_comment: THE shared behavioural contract for the field-lifecycle and blackout RPCs.
Round 2 made the mock and the migration one contract for the affected-booking
KIND LITERALS, by parsing them out of the migration text. That worked because
the literals are text in one file. RPC BEHAVIOUR is not: it lives in PL/pgSQL
on one side and JavaScript on the other, and no amount of parsing turns one
into the other. So round 2's fixes to admin_retire_field and
admin_unretire_field landed in the SQL and not in the mock, and round 3 found
both -- one of them CERTIFIED by a passing test.
A per-field diff would not have caught them either; the next divergence is a
field nobody thought to diff. What is shared instead is the OUTCOME: this file
lists cases and what each must produce, and both implementations are run
against it and asserted to agree with THIS, not with each other.
* tests/fieldLifecycleScenarios.test.js   runs them against the mock client
* scripts/dbharness/scenarios.py          emits SQL that runs them against
Postgres, invoked by run.sh
Dates are relative to the day of the run, as offsets in days from today, so
both sides compute the same absolute date and no scenario expires. `null` is
an unbounded window. Every field named here is pseudonymous.
Breaking either side must fail the case, in both harnesses. That is proved:
scripts/dbharness/prove.sh plants against the SQL and the mutation sweep
against the mock.
REFUSAL CONTRACT. A scenario expecting `ok:false` names the SQLSTATE it must
be refused WITH, in `expect.sqlstate`. Both runners check it, so a row
refused for an unrelated reason -- the caller lost its admin role (42501), or
the field id did not resolve (P0002) -- fails instead of scoring as a pass.
The JS runner used to accept ANY error while the SQL runner restricted the
class, so five blackout cases could have stopped exercising their constraint
and stayed green. The mock now carries `error.code`, which is what PostgREST
puts there, so one contract is expressible for both.

fieldScenarios.why: A retirement dated ahead leaves the field live until it arrives.
A retirement already in the past deactivates on the spot.
Inclusive on the end date: retired FOR today is still live today.
HIGH 1. Retiring something is not a way to un-deactivate it. The mock wrote active:true unconditionally and handed a deactivated field back to the scheduler.
Same, with a past date: still false, by both terms of the conjunction.
Re-retiring an already future-retired field moves the date and keeps it live.
Clears the date; the field was live and stays live.

HIGH 2. The field is inactive BECAUSE the retirement passed. Unretire clears the date and leaves activity alone -- it cannot know whether the deactivation was the retirement's doing. Re-activating is admin_update_field.
HIGH 2, the sharpest form. Nobody ever retired this field; it was simply switched off. Unretiring it must not switch it back on. The suite asserted active===true here and so certified the bug.
The no-op direction. An active, undated field is unchanged.

`expect.ok` was shape-validated on all 19 scenarios and read by neither runner for a field scenario -- a field parsed and never read, in the table whose premise is that both runners read it identically. It is load-bearing now: this is the one field case that must be REFUSED, so an `ok` branch that vanished would fail here.

blackoutScenarios.why: Minutes past midnight, both bounds present.
num_nonnulls(location_id, field_id) = 1: exactly one, never both.
The reason is a closed enum, so free text cannot arrive through it.
Both minutes or neither; one alone is a window with no other end.
